pages.x: Cuban rebels had fought Spain for ten years from 1868, and failed. In 1895 they rose again, led by the poet José Martí. Spain sent 200,000 soldiers, and its general, Valeriano Weyler, herded country families into guarded camps to cut the rebels off from their people.

Martí had spent years in exile in New York, writing and gathering Cubans for a new war. He landed with the rebels in 1895, and was shot dead in one of the first battles, at Dos Ríos. Cubans honour him as the Apostle of their independence.

In Weyler's camps well over 100,000 Cubans died of hunger and disease. American newspapers, racing each other for readers, filled their front pages with the horrors, true and invented, and many Americans demanded that their country step in.
pages.of: Cubans who died in the camps

pages.x: On 15 February 1898 the American battleship Maine blew up in Havana harbour, killing more than 260 of her crew. The newspapers blamed Spain, and the cry went up: Remember the Maine! In April Congress declared war. The cause of the blast was never settled; it may have been a fire on board.

The first blow fell on the other side of the world. On 1 May Commodore George Dewey steamed into Manila Bay, in the Philippines, and destroyed the older Spanish fleet there in a morning, without losing a ship. "You may fire when you are ready, Gridley," he told the captain of his flagship.

Theodore Roosevelt quit the navy department to fight. On 1 July his volunteer cavalry, the Rough Riders, cowboys and college men side by side, charged up Kettle Hill with Black regular troops, as the army stormed the San Juan Heights above Santiago de Cuba. It made him a hero, and in 1901 president.

On 3 July the Spanish squadron in Santiago harbour tried to break out to sea, and the waiting American fleet destroyed every ship in a few hours. The city surrendered on 17 July. Far more American soldiers died of yellow fever, malaria and typhoid than of Spanish bullets.

An armistice was signed on 12 August. By the Treaty of Paris in December, Spain gave up Cuba, which the Americans occupied until 1902, and handed Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States, the Philippines for 20 million dollars.

In the Philippines, Emilio Aguinaldo's rebels had fought Spain alongside the Americans, and declared independence in June 1898. When the United States kept the islands, war broke out between them in February 1899. It lasted over three years and killed at least 200,000 Filipinos, most of them civilians.

The war made the United States a power with an empire across the Pacific, and Cuba a nation, though under American watch for decades. For Spain it was simply the Disaster: the loss of the last great pieces of an empire four centuries old, which set its writers and thinkers asking what had gone wrong.
pts: Spain lost the last of its empire
The United States became a colonial power
